projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Martha Hollman was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Martha Rareman (ph) Hollman.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: And your date of birth?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: December the 10th, 1907.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Okay. And today's date is April 28, 2002.

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Uh, huh.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: And, we are at? What's --

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: 1320 Southeast Second Street, the Rack Bone (ph).

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: And I am Allison Chandler. We're going to talk a little bit about World War II. You served in the American Air Force here, right?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: First, you were born here, weren't you?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Right in Evansville. And what was your family background?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, they were ordinary people, I would say. My dad worked in a wood in _______ (inaudible) World Furniture Factory for a long time, and my mother was a regular housewife.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: What is your educational background?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Eighth grade, St. Barnabus School. Wright's High School, Walker's Business College.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: And at the time of the war, were you in a relationship? Married or single?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Single.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: And then later on you married, correct?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Later on you became married, right?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Yes; quite a bit later on.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Where did you live or work during the war?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: I lived on West Illinois Street, and I worked at several places. I was supposed to work at the Republic Aviation, and I was at this for about a month, and then I went over to the Halmond (ph) Building and opened an office there for dignitaries that come in for the Air Force. And wile I was there, they needed someone at Serville (ph), and so they asked me to go over, and I stayed there then. It was easier for me to get back and forth from my home to work. I went out to Republic Aviation. I had to take that bus out there and that was a lot of trouble.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Now, what was Serville (ph)?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: The Serville made refrigerators before the war, and it was a huge plant and it's now -- Whirlpool is in that plant, and it was, it was huge. It's - and I stayed there until the war was over. I was - they called us the Material Division of the Army/Air Force.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: So what did you do at Serville?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, I audited all of the books that came in for the Army. We had purchasing and then some things were taken out of Serville's stock that they purchased themselves. Everything had to be gone over once, and maybe two or three times for errors and anything, anything at all. And sometimes we'd get a stack like that high to do in one day, and anything that's pertained to the wing is what we made in Evansville. The wings that went on the B-47 planes. But I'd -- we had -- they worked around the clock,and we did and Republic Aviation did, now I don't know which made which parts that I did see some of the workers out there as I went through the plant, and then the wings were assembled. And they were all shipped out of Evansville on a big rail at night, and they went to - I can't remember now where that was where they went. Well, they -- they went quite a distance away from here to be put on the planes, and the B-47 was a nice fighter plane. It was strong, and I read in the paper, I believe it was, they were going to bring a couple of the B-47 back to Evansville this summer.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: That would be interesting.

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Why did you choose to become part of the Army at this point?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, I could have stayed in, but I had to go out of town or go wherever they wanted me to go, and I just didn't want to leave the family. My mother wasn't well at that time, and I didn't want to get to far away, so I had to drop out.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Did you have to have special training for your job?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, they trained us out at Republican Aviation before I opened up that other office, and we had a lot of manuals we had to read. And so that's all the training I had, except I was - I was a bookkeeper for 16 years before I took what I'm -- I quit my job because I knew they weren't going to do it make any work things, and I - I was there 16 years, and so I was an accountant and that's what I went in the Army/Air Force. And I had good ratings. We were rated by the Army/Air Force from our major that came in once a month, and my ratings were always very good. So I guess I - I guess I did all right.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Did you have a lot of friendships at work?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Yes, um hum.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: When I worked for Serville.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: - did you maintain friendships with them afterwards,after you quit? Did you stay friends?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: No, we all went our own way. I got another position after that, and I went over to WBGF. I worked in the radio station for about four-and a-half years.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Were you unionized? I guess you wouldn't be unionized since you worked for the Army, would you?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: No, no union; uh-uh, nothing like that.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: How did you feel about the war?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, actually I don't know. We just kept working.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Did the war change any of your activities? Like what you did for fun?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, Serville had a little band of their own, and they had a little place in the country where they had picnics and all. And they always invited us. And then we used to go to Breckenridge with - as part of Serville people; and on Sundays and danced. And then Breckenridge had big bands. They brought us all home and that was fun too. One of the little girl's mother wouldn't - didn't want her to go unless I went along because I was older than she was, and so she - she'd pass my desk about half a dozen times a day. "Are you going with us?" Are you going with us?" I have to say, "Yes." We did all right.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Had fun, still?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Did you take on like different responsibilities once the war started?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, we had enough right there. I went home at nights. I -- we all did. A lot of the people that worked with us were from Indianapolis that were sent down here before I went over there, and we sort of - we worked in pairs; a man and one of the ladies, and we did different things in the office. But I had -- when I -- I was up for -- see - what did they call that - a seven rating, and went in as a two. So I went up pretty far and that was the highest one there. We did the main audit, the man that I worked with and myself.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Were you or any others in your community treated differently because of your gender or race or any other factor?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Everyone was pretty much treated fair?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: No. Everything went fine.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: That's always nice to hear.

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: What was your most memorable experience from working in the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, I guess we were too busy to even think what that would be. I went in because they were going -- they were going to just draft the single women after they had drafted the men. And I was just at the age where I knew I'd drafted, so I would rather do what I knew how to do is to go in and do something that I did know how to do. So that's the way it started. Now, but I did office work, bookkeeping. And most of the time, I liked that better than I did stenographer work.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: What is stenographer work?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, you took letters by shorthand and typed them, and we had dictaphone machines at that time, and I -- I worked at the Advance Store (ph) Works for the 16 years and when the stenographers were sick or something, why I had to do their work too and then go back and do mine.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Double duty?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Did you know anyone who was fighting during the war? Just neighborhood boys or something?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well lots. Some of the young men that we used to date, go to dances with. I just - one of them didn't back.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Only one?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: That's pretty good.

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: I think so, too.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Was anyone in the family involved with the war efforts?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, my two brothers. We were all single at that time. They went to be examined and each -- they went three different times, and each time they said they have high blood pressure, and they didn't take them. And so they had quit their jobs, and my brother sold his car and everything because he thought, you know, he had to go, and they didn't have to go, just me.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Did they get jobs like you did? Working in the offices?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: One of them worked at the shipyard, and he painted the hull of the ships. And my other brother took a job as managing a place where they ate and drank at the -- let's see what they, what they call it - well, it was downtown so he went back to his job after that was over.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Were you still living at home whenever you were working with the Air Force?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Were you still living at home?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Were your brothers also at home?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Yeah, we did.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Must have been fun?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Let's see here. Were you -- at the end of the war, what did you think?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, at the end of war, I -- I didn't -- as I said, I could have stayed with the Army, I but I didn't. And later on I got -- I went to work over at WBGF. We - I did a little bit of everything there, too.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Did you ever think we wouldn't win the war?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Oh, yes. I thought we'd win, sure.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: How did you cope with like the short -- shortages? Like having to ration everything?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, it was something we thought we had do so we just did it.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: What things were rationed?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Gasoline was rationed and lots of food was rationed. And we couldn't buy shoes. And when we did buy them, you couldn't get out in the rain. You knew that the soles would come off, and the people that didn't buy Navy shoes would give us their cards, and then we could buy us a pair of shoes. We couldn't buy hose or anything like that. You know, nylons, stocking or anything like that. They were all wrinkled. I don't know what they were made off.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Did you do things like victory gardens to help with the few shortages?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: A garden?

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: A victory garden, yeah?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, we had a little garden at home.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Home grown stuff.

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Did you watch a lot of like the news reels and stuff with the war?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: No, we didn't. We -- we had - just read our paper. And, of course, we just had the radios then, you know it - I don't know why is it wasn't busy when I came home, we had a lot of things to do get ready for the next day.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: How many - how long were your working hours?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: We worked eight hours a day.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Let's see here. Did the communities respond well as a whole?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, so far as I know. Except it was a big change when shipyard went down on the west side because they worked day and night down there, too. And it was just crowded. We couldn't go anyplace. We had to stay, you know, didn't want to stay away from the house very long because people come down there to work from all over the country, I guess, and they just took over. But there wasn't any other place to live so we had to stay. But, it was all right when they left again.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: So did people all of a sudden just start leaving, after the war was over, going back to where they came?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Um-hum, yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Did you meet any people from other places?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Yes. I met some. Some were nice. Most of them were nice, but nothing was permanent. We knew that, so....

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: No lasting friendships?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: How would you describe the way the war changed your life?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, I don't think it changed my life any. It was -we were glad, of course, when it was over. And we just took it for granted. We just went along with what we had to do.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: So, no real effects?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Um-hum. We didn't bother about it too much.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Let's see here, is there one story that you've heard from one of your friends who've came back from the war?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: One, yes. I don't talk about it too much. I don't -I think he got killed.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Oh?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: But that's how I have - I have a letter from him. The last one I had, and he was sent on a mission and that was it.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: That's sad.

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Were the boys who came back, were they like really affected by the war?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: They were different in lots of ways. Uh-huh, especially the one that, who lost his brother. It's sort of pessimistic.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Were there any other special jobs at your work place?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Any what?

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Other special jobs like -

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: No, no. I didn't. I got married later on. Then while I worked at the radio station, but I also worked at Ore/Iron (ph)Company and that was -- that was nice there too, but then I got tired of working and keeping house too, and I quit.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Did you go out and see many movies whenever the war was going on?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Not too many. Actually, we -- I didn't have time. I used to go to Victory and it looks about - now it looks about like it did when we went then, went mostly to keep cool in the summertime. That's it.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Let's see here. Did, like once the war started, were people really afraid around here?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: I don't think so. You didn't hear as many things going on, you know, as you do today. People didn't act like that. They didn't try killing each other and doing things like that. I-- I don't remember ever seeing anything like that. No.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: So you got -- you got quite a few promotions in your job, didn't you?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Um-hum. I had -- I was just about as high as I could get there.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Now, with the people who are still here, were there many weddings during the war?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, there was. They - some people just wanted to rush into it, you know. Why, I don't know. I could have done that too, but I didn't. I thought it was best to wait until it was all over, and I'm glad I did.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Were the weddings still like optimistic?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: No. I don't know. Things were just a little different than they are today.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: The medical care, what was that like during the war?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, let's see. Actually, when I -- they took our good doctors, most of them that were here, and when I went to my doctor to get my examination, he said, "Well you're as healthy as I am." And he said, "They got me this morning." So he had to go too. He come back, though.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Now, was it hard to get into the Air Force? Were there like a lot of procedures that you had to go through?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Well, I signed. I went in on my own accord, and they sent me papers right away, and I -- then they told me to go down and get fingerprinted and they -- then I - they sent me out to Republican Aviation.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Have you visited any memorials from the war? Any World War II memorials?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Do you feel very proud on Veteran's Day?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Yes, I do. They make a little bit more of it now than they did for a long time. Like, we have several veterans here. One told my ________ (inaudible) that was in the Marines, he said he's a tall fellow then the little one, he said he flew an airplane, but I - I don't know. I don't ask him too many questions.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Did you your dad do any part in the war?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Hum?

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Your father?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: No. He was, by that time, he was about ready to retire himself. He work in a little furniture factory. He didn't do very much. You know, he knew how to season the wood and lots of the other people didn't know so that's what he did.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Now, how old were you when you started working with the Air Force?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: How old was I? Well, let's see. Well, I put that down here. I was 18 when I started working at the at the Advance Store (ph) Works (ph), and I was there 16 years.

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Yeah, about 34.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: So mid thirties?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: So, were there a lot of younger girls working there?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: There was three of us that worked in the office, and then in the fall we got a little bit busier. They hired another girl from school that made four.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Were you -- did you guys socialize outside the work activities that they provided for you?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Not really?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Any other things you want to talk about?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: No. I guess that sums its all up. You have to be there to know, you know, see a little bit of it.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: So you worked there how many years in the Air Force?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: In the Air Force? I think the war was four years. A little over four years, I was there.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: Four years?

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Four years, I was there.

sp.speaker: Allison Chandler
sp.p: That's neat. Thank you, Martha. I appreciate this.

sp.speaker: Martha Hollman
sp.p: Thank you.
[Conclusion of Interview]
